1.q: יְשֻׂשׂ֥וּ⁠ם מִדְבָּ֖ר וְ⁠צִיָּ֑ה וְ⁠תָגֵ֧ל עֲרָבָ֛ה וְ⁠תִפְרַ֖ח
1.note: Isaiah is speaking of **The wilderness and the desert** and **the Arabah** as if they were living things that could **rejoice** and **be glad**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The wilderness and the desert will be transformed, and the Arabah will be renewed and blossom]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a crocus** blooms abundantly and beautifully, so will the once-barren land **blossom**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and blossom as abundantly and beautifully as a crocus]

2.note: Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [The Arabah will blossom beautifully]

Isaiah is speaking of the land as if it were a living thing that could **be glad** and sing for joy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the Arabah will cause great gladness and singing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [even rejoicing and singing]

2.q: כְּב֤וֹד הַ⁠לְּבָנוֹן֙ נִתַּן לָ֔⁠הּ הֲדַ֥ר הַ⁠כַּרְמֶ֖ל וְ⁠הַ⁠שָּׁר֑וֹן
2.note: Isaiah is speaking of the lush beauty and fertility of the desert as if it were **The glory of Lebanon** and **the splendor of Carmel and Sharon**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Arabah will become as beautiful as Lebanon and as fertile as Carmel and Sharon]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [What is glorious about Lebanon]

The expression **will be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will give the glory of Lebanon to it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is splendid about Carmel and Sharon]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who is glorious]
The pronoun **They** refers to people in general. Isaiah repeats it for emphasis. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Everyone, all the people, will see]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how splendid our God is]

Isaiah is using the possessive form **our God** to describe a God who is characterized by being the one his people worship. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God we worship]

3.note: Here, **the weak hands** represents people whose strength and courage have failed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [those whose strength has failed]

Here, **the tottering knees** represents people who have grown weak and afraid. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and steady those who are afraid]

4.note: Isaiah is speaking of fearful, anxious people as if they were a **hastening of heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to those who are fearful]

Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your God will come to avenge you]

Isaiah is using the possessive form **your God** to describe a God who is characterized by being the one his hearers worship. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God you worship]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **recompense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with God repaying them]

Isaiah is using the possessive form **the recompense of God** to describe a punishment that is characterized by God being the one who carries it out. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with the punishment God himself carries out]

The pronoun **He** refers to your God, mentioned earlier in this verse. The pronoun is repeated for emphasis. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [He, your God, will come]

5.q: אָ֥ז תִּפָּקַ֖חְנָה עֵינֵ֣י עִוְרִ֑ים וְ⁠אָזְנֵ֥י חֵרְשִׁ֖ים תִּפָּתַֽחְנָה
5.note: For poetic purposes, Isaiah is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates each one as **opened** because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here. Alternate translation: [Then the eyes of the blind will be made to see, and the ears of the deaf will be made to hear]

The expression **will be opened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will open the eyes of the blind]

Isaiah is using the plural adjective **blind** as a noun to mean people of a certain kind. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who have been blind] or [people who have not been able to see]

The expression **will be opened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will open the ears of the deaf]

Isaiah is using the plural adjective **deaf** as a noun to mean people of a certain kind. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who have been deaf] or [people who have not been able to hear]

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a deer** leaps quickly and freely, so will **the lame** person will leap once that person is healed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as a deer leaps quickly and freely, so the lame person will leap]

Isaiah is using the singular adjective **lame** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [anyone who has been lame]

Isaiah is using the **tongue** of a **mute** person to represent that whole person in the act of becoming able to speak and singing joyfully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the mute person will sing joyfully]

Isaiah is using the singular adjective **mute** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [anyone who has been mute]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and streams will break out in the Arabah]

7.note: Isaiah is speaking of the mirage in the harsh, barren desert land as if it were **glaring**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the mirage in the burning wasteland will become a pool] or [the hot, dry land will become a pool]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the thirsty place will become springs of water]
The pronoun **its** refers to the jackals. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the jackals’ lair]

8.note: Isaiah is speaking of a holy way of living as if it were a literal road, **The Way of Holiness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and one will call it the road for those who live holy lives]

Isaiah is using the adjective **unclean** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [People who are unclean]

Some ancient manuscripts read “And a highway and a way will be there.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “And a highway will be there.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

9.note: Isaiah is using the adjective **violent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of animal. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the beasts which act violently]

The expression **will not be found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one will find them there]

Isaiah is using the adjective **redeemed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the people who have been redeemed]

10.note: Isaiah is using the possessive form **the ransomed of Yahweh** to describe people who are characterized by having been ransomed by Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and those whom Yahweh has ransomed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **singing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and come to Zion while they sing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will always be joyful]

Isaiah is speaking of **joy of eternity** as if it were a crown that the people would wear on their heads. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and everlasting joy will be theirs]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They will be glad and joyful]

Isaiah is speaking of **Gladness and joy** as if they were living things that could **overtake** people by chasing after them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Gladness and joy will come upon them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will no longer grieve or sigh]

Isaiah is speaking of **sorrow and sighing** as if they were living things that could **flee**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and sorrow and sighing will be no more]
